Building a custom Shopify app isn’t just about writing code that talks to an API. Rather, it’s a well-structured process, and skipping stages is usually why custom apps end up over budget, insecure, or abandoned a year after launch.

But we all want to know how to build a custom Shopify app, right? So, let’s get the answer to that and understand the process that it actually involves, from requirements through long-term maintenance.

1. Requirements

1. Requirements

Before any development starts with the help of a Shopify app developer, get specific about what the app needs to do, and just as importantly, what it doesn’t. Vague requirements (“something to manage inventory better”) lead to scope creep.

Clear ones (“sync stock levels across three warehouses every 15 minutes”) give developers something concrete to build against. This stage should also identify what systems the app needs to talk to and how urgent real-time data actually needs to be.

2. Architecture

A modern Shopify app typically uses Node.js, React, and a framework like Remix, alongside Shopify’s App Bridge and Polaris design system for anything with an admin UI. The architecture decision here matters: will this run as an embedded app inside the Shopify admin, or as a standalone system that connects via API?

That choice shapes everything that follows, including hosting, authentication, and how merchants interact with it day to day.

3. APIs

Custom apps typically work with Shopify’s Admin API (for store data, orders, and inventory) and, if you’re extending the storefront itself, the Storefront API. Since 2026, the GraphQL Admin API has become the primary integration interface, with the older REST API maintained mainly for backward compatibility. Planning which API endpoints you’ll actually need upfront avoids rework later.

4. Authentication

This is where a recent, important change matters: as of January 1, 2026, Shopify closed the old flow for creating new custom apps directly inside the store admin. New custom apps must now be built and managed through the Shopify Dev Dashboard, and they authenticate using generated client credentials or Admin API access tokens rather than the older admin-based key setup.

Existing custom apps built before this date still work fine, but any new build needs to follow this updated process.

5. Development

This is the core build phase: implementing the actual functionality, connecting to the required APIs, and building whatever admin interface or storefront extension the app needs. Using a proper local development environment (via Shopify CLI) rather than editing live is standard practice here; mistakes in a custom app can affect real store data.

6. Testing

Test against a development store before anything touches your live store. This should cover normal use cases and edge cases: what happens during an API rate limit, a failed sync, or unexpected data formats. Testing is also about confirming the app behaves correctly under real order volume, not just in a clean demo environment.

7. Deployment

Once tested, the app gets installed on your live store via an install link generated through the Dev Dashboard. Deployment should include a rollback plan; if something breaks post-launch, you want a clear way to disable or revert the app without disrupting store operations.

8. Maintenance

This is the stage most often skipped in planning, and the one that causes the most long-term pain. APIs change, Shopify updates its platform, and business needs evolve. A custom app with no maintenance plan tends to quietly break as the platform moves forward around it. Before you build, decide who’s responsible for updates and monitoring once the app is live, not after something stops working.

Why This Process Matters

Every stage here exists because skipping it creates a specific, predictable problem later: vague requirements become scope creep, skipped testing becomes a broken checkout, and no maintenance plan becomes an app that quietly fails six months in.

The Bottom Line

Custom Shopify app development is a real piece of work, and not just a quick admin tweak. Treating it with a proper development lifecycle, from requirements through maintenance, is what determines whether it becomes a lasting asset or a liability.

Already decided custom is the right call, or still weighing it against an App Store solution? Our breakdown of Shopify custom app vs app store app can help you confirm that decision before committing to a full build.
